subtype: Approach: linking the chore to something he does anyway [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Anand came home, kicked his shoes under the sofa and dropped his school bag by the door. Payal, his older sister, tripped over it and groaned. "Every single day, Anand."
Wednesday: Pulling on his home shorts, Anand stopped halfway. "I always change the minute I walk in," he thought. "I never forget that part. So what if the shoes go on the rack right after I change? Then the bag goes on the hook. Same order every time, no remembering needed."
The next Monday: He had missed the bag only once all week. Payal came into the hall, looked at the empty floor and raised her eyebrows. "Who cleaned up?"

qa.q: What does Anand say he never forgets to do when he walks in?
qa.a: He says he always changes the minute he walks in and never forgets that part.

qa.q: What does Anand's thinking on Wednesday suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He sounds hopeful and a little pleased with himself, because he has found a habit he never misses and can hang the new jobs onto it.

qa.q: What else could Anand try if the chain slips on a busy day, and why?
qa.a: He could stick a small drawing of shoes and a bag on the inside of the door, because a reminder at the exact spot catches the days when the habit alone fails.

qa.q: How does the new routine look to Payal?
qa.a: Payal is surprised to find the hall clear, and probably relieved that she no longer trips over his bag every evening.

grounding: It shows a boy attaching two small tidying jobs to the change of clothes he does every day so that he forgets them less.

subtype: Approach: linking the chore to something he does anyway [Thinking]
passage: Swati, beti, your sandals are in the kitchen again. Sit, let your Dada Nilesh tell you something. When I was a boy in Nashik, I lost one chappal every week. My mother scolded me each evening, and I felt small, because I did want to be good. One day I noticed something. Every evening, the first thing I did was wash my feet at the tap by the door; Amma would not let anyone in otherwise, so I never skipped it. I thought, the tap is my bell. Feet washed, then chappals under the bench, then satchel on the nail. Tap, bench, nail. I said it in my head for a week. After a month my hands did it without me. Amma stopped scolding. Now, beti, what do you always do when you come in?

qa.a: Young Nilesh washed his feet at the tap by the door.

qa.a: Young Nilesh could have asked Amma to remind him for the first few days, or kept a basket right beside the tap, so the job was impossible to walk past.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's Amma have seen the change in him?
qa.a: Amma would have been pleased and surprised to find the chappals under the bench every evening, with no need to scold.

subtype: Approach: noticing a chore keeps piling up and finding why [Revision]
passage: The heap around Pablo's laundry basket had spread onto the floor again, and his dad, Paulo, held up a sock with two fingers. "Washing day, amigo." Pablo started sorting and frowned. Most of the heap had not come from the basket at all. It came off his desk chair, where his jumper, jeans and school shirt landed every evening. The basket stood far away by the door, so the chair had become a second basket, and on washing day both piles crashed together into one overflowing mess. On Sunday Pablo dragged the basket across the room and wedged it beside the chair. That week, clothes dropped straight in. The next Saturday Paulo found one tidy load and a single stray sock under the bed.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to show the right way [Revision]
passage:
Note for Damini's class teacher, for the Helping at Home sheet
On Thursday Damini swept the verandah by herself. She worked hard, but when she finished there were still grey lines of dust and little heaps she had pushed around. She sat on the step with a sad face and said, "I did it all and it's still dirty." After a minute she came and asked me to show her the proper way. I showed her how to start from the walls and make short strokes toward one corner, keeping the broom low so dust does not fly, then hold the dustpan flat and brush the heap in once. She tried it on the kitchen floor. On Saturday she finished the verandah in half her old time, and it was clean.
- Damini's Dadi, Hansa

qa.q: Where did Damini sweep by herself on Thursday?
qa.a: Damini swept the verandah by herself on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she sat on the step after sweeping?

qa.a: She could break the floor into small sections and finish one at a time, because that shows her which parts are really done.

qa.q: How might the Saturday sweeping look to Dadi Hansa?
qa.a: Dadi sees Damini finish in half the time with a clean floor, and is likely proud that asking for help paid off.

grounding: It shows a girl who still leaves dust after sweeping, asking her grandmother for the right technique and then needing far less effort.

Sunday
Dear diary, today I swept the whole hall for the pooja guests. It took forever and my arm ached. Then Bhupen walked across in his white socks and held his feet up at me. Grey. I nearly cried. I was so fed up of doing it wrong that I went to the kitchen and asked Ammamma to show me properly. She took the broom and swept in short strokes from the walls into one corner, keeping it low, and then pushed the little heap into the dustpan in one go. "Your turn, good girl, Kiran," she said. I did the bedroom her way. It was done in about half the time and my arm didn't hurt. After lunch Bhupen checked his socks again. White!
- Kiran

subtype: Approach: trying and falling and trying again [Action]
passage: From my balcony I watched Jagdish from the ground floor take his friend Baljeet's old cycle, the one with no training wheels, out to the colony lane on Sunday. First try: two pedals, a wobble, and he tipped sideways into the hedge. He got up, brushed his knee and walked the cycle back to the lamp post. The second try went a little further. On the fourth, he fell hard and sat on the kerb for a while, holding his knee. I couldn't tell if he was about to cry or just catching his breath. Baljeet shouted, "Again!" He got back on. By evening he was reaching the gate before putting a foot down. On Wednesday there was a plaster on the knee, and he was out again, riding past the gate.

qa.a: He could wear a helmet and knee pads and practise on grass, so each fall costs less while he still learns balance by trying again.

qa.a: Baljeet seems to enjoy it and wants Jagdish to keep going, shouting "Again!" to push him back on the cycle.

Friday: Arnab's cousin Nitin wheeled out the tall cycle. "No side wheels?" Arnab asked. "None." Arnab pushed off, pedalled three times and crashed into Nani's marigold pots. He sat in the soil, staring at his scraped palms.
Saturday: Palms taped up, Arnab tried again and again in the courtyard. Each time he counted how long before a foot hit the ground: two seconds, three, once five. He fell twice more and got up both times without a word.
Tuesday: The scabs were drying. He still gripped the handles too tightly at the start, but he rode the full length of the courtyard and turned without a foot down. Nitin clapped. Arnab said "Again," before anyone could ask.

subtype: Approach: having a parent hold the seat and let go [Action]
passage:
Mummy, you missed it, so I am writing it down for you before I forget.
This evening in the park, Yamini's papa jogged behind her holding the back of the seat, the way we planned. First round his hand gripped tight; second round only his fingertips. She kept calling, "Don't let go, Papa!" and he kept answering, "I've got you." On the third round he slowed, opened his hand and stopped running. She rode on alone past the swings. Then she looked back, saw him far behind, wobbled and put her feet down, grinning and shaking at once. We had her go twice more, with him letting go sooner each time. Tomorrow we will try starting without his hand at all.
- Alka

qa.a: She rode on alone past the swings.

qa.a: Letting go may have made him nervous, but seeing her ride on past the swings would have made him proud and relieved.

Tuesday night
Diary, I CAN RIDE. Well, sort of. After school Papa took the blue cycle to the road below the monastery. He ran behind me holding the seat and puffing. I said, "Hold it, hold it!" He said, "Holding!" I pedalled and pedalled and it felt so steady, like being on rails. Then I heard him shout from really far away, "Keep going, Pema!" FAR away. So who was holding? Nobody. Me! I wobbled into the grass when I found out, but I was already past the prayer flags. Deepak uncle from next door clapped from his gate. Papa said, "That's my girl," and his face was all red. Tomorrow I'm going to start by myself.
- Pema

subtype: Approach: looking at the ground right in front of the wheel [Pitfall]
passage: Last week I found out my eyes can steer a cycle. Our lane has one electricity pole right in the middle, and I was so scared of hitting it that I kept staring down at my front tyre, watching it wobble over every stone. The pole got closer at the edge of my eye. I kept thinking, don't hit it, don't hit it. Then bang. My handlebar hit the pole and I scraped my shin on the pedal. My little brother Vaibhav ran over yelling, "Vandana didi, you were looking right at it!" He was right. Whatever I was scared of, my wheel went straight there. Now I have a plaster, a sore shin, and I still don't like that pole.

qa.q: How did the crash look to Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav could see what Vandana could not: that the eyes were fixed on the pole, so it looked obvious and a little funny to him 😅

subtype: Approach: looking at the ground right in front of the wheel [Pitfall]
passage:
Coach's note, Saturday learners' group, park track
Gurpreet rode her second full lap today but kept her chin tucked and her eyes glued to the front tyre. At the bend there is a lamp pole I had pointed out to the group. She said aloud, "I won't hit it, I won't hit it," glanced up at the pole, and her handlebars drifted right toward it. She clipped it and fell onto the grass: one scraped palm, no other injury. She was shaken and cross with herself. After we cleaned the scrape, I set two orange cones past the bend and asked her to look only at them. She managed one slow bend without drifting. Next week the whole group will start with the cones drill.
- Tanuja, coach

subtype: Approach: looking far ahead where he wants to go [Revision]

Farhan's cycle slammed into the housing society's compound wall for the second time that afternoon. He sat on the ground, rubbing his elbow and glaring at the bricks. Vasudha, the older girl from B-wing who rode every evening, leaned over the railing. "Where were you looking?"
"At the wall. So I wouldn't hit it."
"Don't. See the green gate at the end of the lane? Look only at that."
Farhan grumbled but climbed back on. He fixed his eyes on the green gate. The handle seemed to turn by itself, in small gentle corrections instead of jerks. He reached the gate without once touching the wall, then turned round and picked the mango tree at the other end.

qa.a: Vasudha has learned it herself and can see his mistake, so it is easy for her and she is probably pleased when it works.

Sunday: Rehana's toes only reached the ground on tiptoe, and every time she tried to pedal she tipped over. Her brother Rafiq offered to push her. She shook her head.
Tuesday: "The pedals aren't the problem," she told Rafiq, pulling the seat down to the lowest notch. "Staying up is. If I can't stay up, pedalling just makes me fall faster." She walked the cycle along, then pushed with both feet and lifted them, gliding for two seconds. Then three.
Friday: She glided across the whole courtyard with her feet up, counting aloud to seven. "Now," she said, "now I'll try the pedals." The first push went round, then the second.

subtype: Approach: gliding without pedals first to find balance [Thinking]
passage: Pradeep, stop kicking that cycle and come sit with your Nani. You think Ira Nani was born riding? In our village there was one cycle, my father's, big and black, and my feet could not touch the ground from the seat. Every time I tried the pedals I fell, and my brother laughed. So one afternoon I sat under the neem and asked myself which part was hard. Not the pedals. Any fool can push pedals. The hard part was staying up. I borrowed the tailor's daughter's small cycle, let the seat right down so my feet were flat, and pushed along the dirt road, lifting my feet, gliding. A little further each day. Only when I could glide past the well did I try the pedals. It took one go.

qa.q: How might Ira's brother have seen her gliding along the dirt road?
qa.a: Ira's brother may have thought it looked silly at first, then been surprised when Ira rode the first time she tried the pedals.

subtype: Approach: giving up after one bad fall [Pitfall]

Vidya scraped her elbow on the colony road one Sunday and announced at dinner that cycling was "too dangerous for normal people." The pink cycle went behind the water tank. Two weeks later, the girls from her building planned an evening ride to the ice-cream cart two lanes away. Trisha knocked on the door. "Coming? You can ride right behind me."
"I don't ride any more," Vidya said, arms folded.
From the window she watched them go, bells ringing, Trisha waving back. She told herself she didn't care. Then she went to her room and shut the door harder than she meant to. The elbow had healed days ago.

In Room 12 of the junior boys' hostel, Yash's laundry bag was always stuffed so full that the drawstring would not close. Devika ma'am, the warden, had tied it shut for him twice that month. On Thursday, during room check, she tapped his chair. "Why does your uniform live here?"
Yash looked. Every night he undressed sitting on that chair beside his bed, while the laundry bag hung on a hook far away by the door. The clothes piled up on the chair, and before laundry day he crammed the whole pile into the bag at once.
"The bag's in the wrong place," he said slowly. He asked if he could tie it to the back of his chair. The warden nodded. By the next laundry day the bag closed easily.

qa.a: He seemed surprised and then pleased, speaking slowly as the reason became clear to him.

qa.q: What else could Yash try if clothes still pile up on busy nights?
qa.a: He could do a quick check of the chair before lights out each night, because a tiny daily step stops a big pile forming.

qa.q: How does the change look to Devika ma'am?
qa.a: The warden no longer has to tie his bag shut and can see he fixed the cause himself, so she is likely pleased.

grounding: It shows a child who notices his laundry keeps piling up, works out that clothes collect on his chair and moves the bag beside it.
